title: Holi: the festival of colors
hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali and King Bali, who kept his word and comes home once a year. Light the way home.

At the Holi bonfire, Prahlad walks out of the fire. But the story doesn't stop there, and the Bhagavata Purana carries it further. His father, the king Hiranyakashipu, has tried everything to kill him, and nothing works. Finally, in a rage, he stands before his son in the great hall and asks: this Vishnu of yours, who you say is everywhere. Is he in this pillar? The boy says yes. And the king strikes the pillar.
screen: `THE FIRE WAS NOT THE END.` → `IS HE IN THIS PILLAR?` → `THE KING STRIKES IT.`

segments.voice: To understand what happens next, you need the king's boon. Long before, after fierce austerities, Hiranyakashipu had been granted protection, as the Bhagavata tells it, with a long list of conditions. No man or animal could kill him. Not by day or by night. Not inside or outside. Not on the earth or in the sky. Not with any weapon. He thought he'd closed every door. When he strikes the pillar, it splits open, and out comes Narasimha: Vishnu as half man, half lion. Neither man nor animal. He seizes the king at twilight, neither day nor night; on the threshold of the hall, neither inside nor outside; across his lap, neither earth nor sky; and ends him with his claws, which are not a weapon. Every door the king had closed, opened. Narasimha's fury is so terrible that even the gods are afraid to come near. They send the boy. Prahlad walks up and bows, and Narasimha calms and puts his hand on his head. Offered any blessing he wants, Prahlad asks for something astonishing: that his father, who tried to kill him again and again, be purified and freed. The Bhagavata says the wish is granted. Some readers hear in it a key to the morning of colors: the boy who survived everything asks not for revenge but for his father's release. In some villages, people roast ears of new wheat or barley in the Holi bonfire and share them: fresh grain, cooked in the fire that ended the cruelty, eaten together.
screen: `NOT MAN OR BEAST, NOT DAY OR NIGHT.` · `NARASIMHA BURSTS FROM THE PILLAR.` · `ONLY THE BOY CAN CALM HIM.` · `PRAHLAD ASKS FOR HIS FATHER'S RELEASE.` · then, large: `NOT REVENGE, BUT RELEASE.`

segments.voice: Bring back the small grudge you set on the fire a couple of weeks ago, or a new one. Try what Prahlad did, just a little: not forgiving everything, only wishing the other person well for one breath, may they be free of whatever made them act that way. Then let it go with the out-breath.
Holi. The fire for Prahlad, Narasimha from the pillar, and a boy who asked not for revenge but for his father's release.
Your line: everyone's the same color today. Tomorrow, a column of fire with no end. Rest well.

howItsDone: At Holika Dahan, some communities roast ears of new wheat or barley in the bonfire and share them; the next morning, Holi is often a day for visiting, reconciling and starting fresh with neighbors and relatives.
